 By Monica Casey, WRAL Durham Reporter
 For the first time since the guilty verdict, SBI agents who helped catch Faith Hedgepeth's killer are speaking about their investigation.
 Miguel Salguero-Olivares was found guilty of Hedgepeth's murder on October 23rd.
 Other WRAL Top Stories
 Hedgepeth was killed in 2012; Phillip Stevens and Justin Heinrich joined the investigation in 2013.
 Stevens is now the Assistant Director of the SBI, and Heinrich is the Special Agent in Charge of Special Operations.
 Chapel Hill Police asked for the SBI’s assistance around the one-year anniversary of Hedgepeth’s death.
 Stevens and Heinrich described the investigation as all-consuming.
 “It would be the last thing I would think about going to bed, waking up in the morning,” Stevens said. “I would dream about this case.”
 Stevens and Heinrich say they decided to review CHPD’s initial files separately, and both agreed CHPD had done a “phenomenal job.” 
 “It was just that there was an opportunity to go more in depth and use maybe more technology, more kind of outside the box thinking with our investigative approach,” Stevens said.
 In particular, they were able to obtain significantly more data from Faith Hedgepeth’s phone, taking about 100 pages of information to closer to 5,000 pages.  
 More than 25 agents were assigned to assist in the case.
 “We've swabbed over 400 people. We interviewed probably over 100 people. Thousands of man-hours went into this case,” Stevens said.  
 “The scope of this case was unlike anything else that I've ever personally worked,” Heinrich said. 
 Stevens said the case was made more difficult to solve by the lack of relationship between Hedgepeth and Salguero-Olivares.
 “If there's no connection between your victim and your suspect, it can be almost impossible to find out who that person is, a needle in a haystack,” Stevens said. “Usually 99% of the homicides that I've worked in my career, there was a clear connection between the victim and the suspect.”
 Stevens taught the case to SBI trainees while it was unsolved, in part because they were closer to Hedgepeth's age
 “They would give me leads, and I would take that in the field, and I would follow them down,” he said.
 Then, in 2021, an investigative genealogical DNA match was made to Miguel Salguero-Olivares.
 “The phone call we got from the lab telling us that we had a DNA match was a feeling that I'll never experience again. It was so satisfying. All the hours of hard work that everyone did on the team finally paid off,” Stevens said. “But also, there was a sense of urgency when we got our person. We didn't sleep that night.”
 Heinrich said investigators never gave up, with someone working on the case every day.
 “This was a unique case in that we never really got to that point where there wasn't a lead to follow. Some people call this a cold case because it's 14 years old, and we've talked, and I wouldn't consider this a cold case because there was always active work being done on this,” Heinrich said.
 Now, new trainees at the SBI learn from their success.
 “We try to impart in future generations of agents, is to approach that case and try to think outside the box and pursue investigative techniques that you know might not be conventional. Don't just do what worked in the last few cases,” Heinrich said.
 "The lesson that we learn, and what I teach in this in our academy, is it's so important to document every single thing, because in this case, it was 14 years later," Stevens said. "I was reading interviews, preparing for trial that I didn't even remember doing."
 Salguero-Olivares was found guilty of all four charges he faced: murder, rape, sex offense, and burglary.
 Hedgepeth's family offered forgiveness to her killer and thanks to the investigators who put him behind bars.
 “I wasn't surprised by what they said. They had demonstrated that throughout this entire process, they could have easily gotten frustrated at us,” Stevens said. “They could easily gotten upset with us, and they stayed consistent throughout this process. They were supportive. They understood that this may take time.”
 “I was holding Rolanda's hand throughout the verdict being read,” Heinrich said. “The grace that they live with, it's amazing,” Heinrich said. “It's something to behold, and I'm glad that the public could see what we've seen for years.”
